sections.title: Names, a wider people and a present Nation
sections.text: The Comanche Nation uses Nʉmʉnʉʉ for its people. Its own historical account connects movement onto the Plains with horse-based life and kinship-based bands. This people-level directory route and the present government are related levels of description, rather than one unchanged organization across all periods. Current membership numbers and governing rules require separate dated verification.

sections.title: Bands need their own context
sections.text: The consulted TxDOT report describes changing local bands and wider divisions, with relationships that could form and change. Penateka, Nokoni and Quahadi are among its historical labels. These names should remain individually searchable when their identities and aliases are checked; a list of bands does not prove that each is a separate present government.

sections.title: Plains movement and Texas history
sections.text: The Nation’s account follows movement southward and emphasizes horses and bison. TxDOT’s selected historical chapters connect Texas history to military pressure and removal to reservation life. These broad accounts provide a starting chronology, not precise homeland boundaries. The report contains internal date problems that remain disclosed in its source card.

sections.title: Reading the 1867 treaty critically
sections.text: The Medicine Lodge treaty transcription contains a reservation provision, a reserved hunting clause and a consent requirement for later cession of reservation land. It also sets out federal services and compulsory English-school attendance. The text places promises of protection and services alongside compulsory schooling and requirements to make the reservation a permanent home. The wording alone does not establish implementation, universal agreement or present-day legal rights.

sections.title: Community-directed language institutions
sections.text: The Language Department’s account traces its planning to community organizing in 2017 and funding for fiscal 2019. It recognizes the earlier preservation committee and describes teacher certification, curriculum and digital resources among its goals. These are the department’s reported history and aims; this review did not test an app, inspect a curriculum or measure fluency.

sections.title: A dated record of teaching across communities
sections.text: Fuentes’s 1999 source book records preservation work and a Toya Band language class in Albuquerque and Santa Fe. It describes volunteer teaching, intergenerational participation and materials in that historical setting. The two program entries form one reviewed educational work. They do not establish today’s schedule, participation or separate-government status.

sections.title: Language, family memory and individual experience
sections.text: The Boulder report presents Ruth Toathy’s and Rosemary Chibity’s differing memories of language use at home and pressure toward English, alongside Leonard Chibity’s comments on place names. These are named personal accounts within an edited public report. They help readers see lived experiences without turning one recollection into a statement about every Comanche family.

sections.title: What this foundation still needs
sections.text: Six inspected works provide a starting source guide. More Comanche-authored historical scholarship, primary records of Texas negotiations and displacement, and careful comparison of band names remain needed. Several selected texts are institutional or edited accounts; no community review is recorded. The older university volume remains an unread lead, and the cultural index does not count toward the substantive total.

overview: Comanche people’s histories connect the Southern Plains, Texas and the present Comanche Nation in Oklahoma. This foundation brings the Nation’s own account together with community-directed language history, a consulted Texas report, an edited treaty and attributed educational accounts. Historical bands, the broader people and the present government retain their own contexts.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Six directly relevant works have actual selected-content inspection. They establish a useful foundation, but community-authored historical depth, Texas primary records and band-level identity comparisons remain uneven. No comprehensive history, current legal assessment or community endorsement is claimed.
remainingLimits: Selected-page and selected-section review does not imply complete reading of each volume.
Underlying treaty manuscript, negotiations, implementation and later legal interpretation remain unreviewed.
TxDOT internal chronology and evaluative interpretations require comparison rather than automatic adoption.
The 1999 education record is historical; current program outcomes and language-use counts are not verified.
No community review or endorsement is recorded.
